---
title: "6. Classify habitat type (Random Forest)"
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

*Use Random Forest to classify habitat type from community composition data.*

Here we train a classifier that predicts the habitat type of a sample from its arthropod community composition. Good classification accuracy suggests that the community composition is a reliable indicator of habitat.

### Choose target variable

We use habitat type as the target:

```r
y <- as.factor(habitat)
```

Remove samples with missing habitat labels:

```r
ok <- which(!is.na(y))
y  <- y[ok]
```

### Create a feature matrix

We use relative abundances of ASVs as features (`norm_sparse` created in [4](tutorial-04-pcoa.qmd)).
By filtering rare ASVs in sparse space before converting to dense, we avoid creating a large intermediate matrix:

```r
X_sparse <- Matrix::t(norm_sparse)[ok, , drop = FALSE]  # samples × ASVs (sparse)

# Filter ASVs present in <10% of samples
keep <- which(Matrix::colSums(X_sparse > 0) / nrow(X_sparse) >= 0.1)

# Convert to dense only after filtering
X <- as.matrix(X_sparse[, keep, drop = FALSE])
```

### Train/test split

Split the data into training and test sets to evaluate model performance on unseen samples.

```r
set.seed(1)
n         <- nrow(X)
train_ix  <- sample(seq_len(n), size = round(0.8 * n))
test_ix   <- setdiff(seq_len(n), train_ix)

X_train <- X[train_ix, , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- y[train_ix]

X_test  <- X[test_ix, , drop = FALSE]
y_test  <- y[test_ix]
```

### Train Random Forest

We train a [random forest classifier](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/r-language/random-forest-approach-in-r-programming/){target="_blank"} using the R package ranger.

```r
rf <- ranger(
  x          = X_train,
  y          = y_train,
  num.trees  = 500,
  importance = "permutation"
)
```

500 trees gives a good balance between accuracy and runtime for tutorial datasets. For production models, increasing to 1000–5000 trees can improve stability.

### Predict and evaluate

Assess model performance by predicting habitat type for the test data.

```r
pred <- predict(rf, data = X_test)$predictions

# Overall accuracy
mean(pred == y_test)

# Confusion matrix
table(Predicted = pred, Observed = y_test)
```

A confusion matrix shows which habitat types are correctly classified and which are confused with each other. High off-diagonal values for a pair of habitats suggest their arthropod communities are similar.

### Variable importance (optional)

Identify which ASVs contribute most to habitat classification.

```r
imp <- sort(rf$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)
plot(imp, xlab = "ASV rank", ylab = "Permutation importance")
```

To get the taxonomy of the 10 most important ASVs:

```r
merged_df$asvs[names(imp[1:10]), 7:10]
```
